newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem scorns Argentine unions' "total" strike claim.
newsitem.headline: Menem scorns Argentine unions' "total" strike claim.

text.p: Trade unions hailed their 36-hour general strike as a total success on Friday, accusing President Carlos Menem of blinding himself to the suffering of Argentines by dismissing the protest as a "complete failure."

Unions said the walkout from noon (1500 GMT) Thursday in protest of 17.1 percent unemployment and the Peronists' drive for fiscal austerity, cuts in worker benefits and new labour laws that benefit employers, had a 90 percent success rate.

"The strike is an absolute success because the people have joined in," proclaimed Rodolfo Daer, head of the main labour federation, the CGT. Once a Peronist ally but now on its third general strike in a year, the CGT accused Menem of betraying the Peronist movement and robbing workers of job security.
It said 100,000 people filled the Plaza de Mayo Thursday.

But Menem said the protest on the doorstep of his Casa Rosada presidential palace drew only 40,000 people and joked that Sunday's big soccer match between Boca Juniors and River Plate would draw a bigger crowd.

"In my opinion it was a complete failure. In a city of 3.5 million people, ruled by the Radicals, for a protest of all the opposition and the CGT to get no more than 40,000 people according to police is a failure," he told Clarin newspaper.
Interviewed by La Nacion, he vowed to push ahead on labour reforms and said the strike "changes nothing in any way. These demands don't scare anybody, least of all the government."

Menem said on radio the unions wanted to drag Argentina "back to a country of hyperinflation and widespread corruption," referring to his success in reducing inflation to zero from 5,000 percent and privatising corruption-ridden state firms since he first came to power in 1989.

With cities empty of buses, airports and ports disrupted and banks and financial markets doing thin business, however, Labour Minister Armando Caro Figueroa said the protest was a "major demonstration of a certain climate of unhappiness."

Menem said the view from his helicopter flying over Buenos Aires was "really pathetic." But Daer said that kind of dismissive attitude "shows he doesn't know where he is living nor what is going on in the life of ordinary Argentines."
Regretting that he and many CGT members voted Menem back for a second term in 1995, Daer accused the 66-year-old leader of betraying his election promise to "pulverize" unemployment.

"Workers, the labour movement and all major social sectors supported the president because he told us in two or three years we'd be on the road to greatness," Daer said. "Years have passed and rather than the road to glory we're on the road to social inequalities deeper than ever in our history."

The head of the Catholic charity Caritas, Bishop Rafael Rey, warned the government: "After the strike nobody can look the other way. This was not in support of the CGT or union leaders but a cry of pain from people starved of jobs."

In Rosario, a once wealthy city west of Buenos Aires hard hit by unemployment, a group of priests and monks were fasting in sympathy with the strikers. One of them, Father Jorge Aloi, urged "the political leadership to wake up to the grave situation the inhabitants of Argentina are living through."
